note: Step format and conventions: see README.md.

scenarios.description: A creates a task; B pulls it. Pull is state-based and carries the epoch.
Replaying an op id returns the stored result, even after the task has changed since.
Create of a live id: identical content is a no-op, different content is rejected.
An update on the current revision is applied.
Concurrent edits to different field groups both survive.
Concurrent edits to the same group: the later arrival wins and the loser is recorded.
Two devices setting the same value do not conflict and consume no sequence number.
completed and completed_at move together as one group.
A delete on the current revision becomes a content-free tombstone.
Two devices purging the same task: the second delete is a no-op.
A deliberate edit made before the delete was seen brings the task back, with a conflict record.
A delete based on an older revision loses to a newer edit (edit wins).
Presence is not an edit: a create never resurrects a deleted id.
base_rev must not be ahead of the server, nor at or past a tombstone.
Restore (undo, or an explicit keep) needs the tombstone's exact revision.
Update, delete and restore of an id the server never saw are rejected.
Field limits, trimming and malformed ops. Rejected ops consume no sequence number.
created_at and completed_at are clamped by the server and reported in adjusted.
The account-wide cleanup policy is a synced setting with the same conflict rules.
Pages are contiguous in seq order; has_more is true until the head is reached.
A task changed several times is returned once, at its latest revision.
Ids are scoped to the account; another account sees and affects nothing.
One rejected op does not stop the rest of the batch.
A resurrection notice reaches a device even if the task changed again before it pulled.
Only the first two operations of a batch committed before the connection dropped; re-sending the identical batch replays them and applies the rest.
The answer to an applied update was lost and another device changed the same field afterwards; the byte-identical replay returns the stored result and changes nothing.

Why an unknown-outcome update must never be re-sent under a new op_id: the new copy collides and overwrites the newer value (a conflict is stored, but data moved). Clients reconcile instead (SYNC 11.6).
A rejected operation replays as the same rejection even after the state would now accept it.
Restore carries the full task, which is validated like a create; created_at comes from the tombstone; the base must be the current tombstone rev.
A resurrecting update is validated in full, keeps created_at from the tombstone, and revisions only ever increase.
An entity delivered on page one and changed before page two is delivered again at its higher seq; nothing is missed and the last page ends at head_seq.
A push result never moves the pull cursor; an empty page ends at head_seq; a cursor ahead of the server is refused with cursor_ahead.
